chapter_note.about: Cache questions are bit-counting and bookkeeping. You are given a cache size, a block size and an address width, and you must split the address, count the storage, price a miss or replay a trace. This chapter starts with memory chips and decoders. Then it covers the address split for direct-mapped and set-associative caches, and the tag directory. After that come average access time, CPI with stalls, write policies, replacement and miss types, block transfer, array locality and DRAM refresh.
chapter_note.simple: A cache is a small, fast notebook that keeps copies of pages from a big, slow library. Every page has a number, and the number is cut into three parts: which shelf, which spot on the shelf, and a label to check it is the right page. This chapter teaches you to cut those numbers correctly. It also shows how to work out the average time of a lookup when most are found in the notebook and a few need a trip to the library. You also learn what happens when the notebook is full, how changes get written back, and why some ways of reading an array cause many extra trips. In exam words: address split, tag directory, AMAT, CPI with stalls, write policies, LRU and FIFO, interleaving, locality and DRAM refresh.

cards.title: Memory chips and decoding
cards.simple: Picture a school library made from identical shelves. Each shelf holds the same number of books. To hold more books you stack more shelves. To make each entry wider, you put two shelves side by side and read both together. A book number has two parts. The first digits say which stack to walk to, and the last digits say the spot on the shelf. In exam words: chips needed = total bits divided by bits per chip. The low address bits go to every chip, and the high bits go through a decoder that switches on one row of chips.
cards.idea: A **memory chip** has a fixed number of words, each a fixed width. To build a bigger memory you join chips. Put chips side by side to make the words wider. Stack rows of chips to get more words. The low address bits go to every chip. The high bits pick which row is switched on.
cards.definition:
To build a $W\times b$ memory from $w\times c$ chips: chips $=\dfrac{W\times b}{w\times c}$, rows $=W/w$, columns $=b/c$.

Here $W$ is the words wanted, $b$ the word width wanted, $w$ the words per chip and $c$ the chip width. The address has $\log_2 W$ bits. Each chip takes the low $\log_2 w$ bits. The remaining $\log_2(\text{rows})$ high bits feed a decoder that drives the chip selects.
cards.intuition_full: A chip is a fixed block of storage: $w$ addresses, each holding $c$ bits. You have two separate shortages to fill. If words must be wider than $c$ bits, you place chips side by side and give them the same address, so each chip supplies part of the word. If you need more addresses than $w$, you stack rows of chips and arrange that only one row answers at a time. A decoder makes that choice. It reads the top address bits and raises exactly one row-select line. Every chip sees the same low bits, so the chip itself picks one of its $w$ words. Think of a hotel. The top digits of a room number pick the floor, the last digits pick the room on that floor, and a double room is two single rooms read together. The chip-count formula is only a shortcut for rows times columns.

examples.setup: Build a $32\text{K}\times16$ memory from $8\text{K}\times8$ chips. How many chips are needed, and which address bits drive the decoder? Which row serves address $\text{0x5A3C}$?
steps: Total bits wanted: $32\text{K}\times16=512$ Kbit. One chip holds $8\text{K}\times8=64$ Kbit. Chips $=512/64=8$.
Rows (more words): $32\text{K}/8\text{K}=4$. Columns (wider words): $16/8=2$. The grid is 4 rows by 2 columns.
$32\text{K}=2^{15}$ words, so the address is $A_{14}\ldots A_0$. Each chip has $8\text{K}=2^{13}$ words, so $A_{12}\ldots A_0$ go to every chip.
The other $15-13=2$ bits, $A_{14}A_{13}$, enter a 2-to-4 decoder. Its four outputs are the four row selects.
$\text{0x5A3C}=101\,1010\,0011\,1100_2$ (15 bits). $A_{14}A_{13}=10_2=2$, so row 2 is on, and $\text{0x1A3C}$ picks the word inside both chips of that row.
examples.answer: 8 chips in 4 rows by 2 columns. $A_{14}A_{13}$ drive the decoder. Row 2 covers $\text{0x4000}$ to $\text{0x5FFF}$, so $\text{0x5A3C}$ is word $\text{0x1A3C}$ of row 2.

examples.setup: A system has 16 address lines $A_{15}\ldots A_0$. An $8\text{K}$-word RAM chip is enabled by $CS=A_{15}\cdot\overline{A_{14}}\cdot A_{13}$, where the bar is a bubble on that input. Find the address range that enables the chip.
steps: The chip has $8\text{K}=2^{13}$ words, so $A_{12}\ldots A_0$ go to the chip. They are free and can be anything.
$CS$ is high only when $A_{15}=1$, $A_{14}=0$ (the bubble inverts it) and $A_{13}=1$. So $A_{15}A_{14}A_{13}=101$.
examples.answer: The chip answers for $\text{0xA000}$ to $\text{0xBFFF}$, exactly 8K addresses. A bubble means that bit must be 0, not 1.

examples.setup: A $24\text{K}\times8$ memory is built from $8\text{K}\times8$ chips on a 15-bit address bus. How many chips, how many decoder inputs, and what happens at $\text{0x6000}$?
steps: Chips $=24\text{K}/8\text{K}=3$, in 3 rows of one column.
Three rows still need $\lceil\log_2 3\rceil=2$ decoder bits, $A_{14}A_{13}$. A 2-to-4 decoder has 4 outputs but only 3 are wired.
$\text{0x6000}=110\,0000\,0000\,0000_2$ gives $A_{14}A_{13}=11$, the unused output. No chip answers there.
examples.answer: 3 chips, a 2-bit decoder, and $\text{0x6000}$ to $\text{0x7FFF}$ is an unmapped hole. The row count need not be a power of 2, but the decoder width is rounded up.

cards.why: This fixes how a CPU address becomes a chip choice. Without it you cannot count chips or say which addresses a chip answers. In GATE: count the chips for a given size, or read a chip-select gate and give the address range it enables.
how: Chips $=$ total bits $\div$ bits per chip.
Rows $=W/w$, columns $=b/c$.
Bits to each chip $=\log_2 w$. The remaining high bits feed the decoder.
For a chip-select gate, set every input to the value that makes it 1 (a bubble means that bit is 0). Free low bits give the range.
cards.mistake: Counting only the word ratio and forgetting the width. A $16\text{K}\times8$ chip cannot make 16-bit words alone, so you also need columns. Another slip is reading a bubble on a gate input as a plain 1.
edge_cases: Rows not a power of 2: the decoder still needs $\lceil\log_2\text{rows}\rceil$ bits and one output stays unused.
Chip wider than the word needed: use part of its width, so the chip count is still $\lceil\cdot\rceil$ of the ratio.
Address range of a row: set the decoded bits, then let the low bits run from all 0 to all 1.
connections: The same decoder idea selects a cache set from the index bits (cards m2 and m3).
Ties to the I/O chapter: devices also get address ranges through a decoder (memory-mapped I/O).

cards.title: Address split in a direct-mapped cache
cards.simple: Think of a hostel with 64 lockers in a row. A student is told a long ID number. The last few digits say which shelf inside the locker to look at. The middle digits say which locker is theirs. The remaining front digits are the name label stuck on the locker door, so you can check that the locker really belongs to this student. A cache address works the same way. In exam words: offset, index and tag. Offset picks the byte in the block, index picks the line, and tag is compared to see if the right block is sitting in that line.
cards.idea: A cache cuts every address into three fields. The low bits are the **offset**, the byte inside a block. The middle bits are the **index**, which picks the cache line. The top bits are the **tag**, stored with the line to prove which block is there. In a direct-mapped cache each block has exactly one possible line.
cards.definition:
$\text{offset}=\log_2(\text{block size})$, $\text{index}=\log_2(\text{lines})$, $\text{tag}=\text{address bits}-\text{index}-\text{offset}$.

Here lines $=\text{cache size}/\text{block size}$. Index plus offset always equals $\log_2(\text{cache size})$, so $\text{tag}=\text{address bits}-\log_2(\text{cache size})$.
cards.intuition_full: Memory is chopped into blocks, and the block is the unit that moves in and out of the cache. The offset only says where to look inside one block, so it needs enough bits for the block size and nothing more. Many blocks compete for each line, so the index says which line a block must use. Blocks that share the same index bits fight over one line. The tag is everything left over. It is stored next to the data because two blocks with the same index differ only in their tag. A hit means the line is valid and its stored tag equals the address tag. Notice that index plus offset covers exactly the bits that one cache-sized region of memory can vary. That is why the tag width depends on the cache size and address size, not on the block size.

examples.setup: A machine has 24-bit byte addresses and a 4 KB direct-mapped cache with 64-byte blocks. Split the address into tag, index and offset, then split $\text{0x3A5C7E}$.
steps: The address has 24 bits. The cache is 4 KB $=2^{12}$ bytes and a block is 64 B $=2^6$ bytes.
Offset $=\log_2 64=6$ bits. The low 6 bits say which byte inside the block.
Lines $=4096/64=64$, so index $=\log_2 64=6$ bits. Direct mapped: sets equal lines.
Tag $=24-6-6=12$ bits. Check: index plus offset $=12=\log_2 4096$.
The block belongs in line 49. A hit needs line 49 to be valid and to hold tag 933.
examples.answer: Tag 12, index 6, offset 6 bits. $\text{0x3A5C7E}$ has tag 933, index 49, offset 62.

examples.setup: A direct-mapped cache has 1024 lines. Addresses are 32 bits and the tag is 18 bits. The block size is not given. Find the block size and the cache size.
steps: Index $=\log_2 1024=10$ bits.
Offset $=32-18-10=4$ bits, so the block is $2^4=16$ bytes.
Cache size $=1024\times16\text{ B}=16\text{ KB}$.
Check: index plus offset $=14=\log_2 16\text{K}$. The tag $=32-14=18$ agrees.
examples.answer: Block size 16 B and cache size 16 KB. GATE hides the block size on purpose; recover it from the leftover bits.

examples.setup: A 16 KB direct-mapped cache on a byte-addressed machine with 32-bit addresses has blocks of 8 words, and a word is 4 bytes. Find the field widths.
steps: Block size in bytes $=8\times4=32$ B, so offset $=\log_2 32=5$ bits. Using 8 would give 3 bits, which is wrong.
Lines $=16\text{K}/32=512$, so index $=9$ bits.
Tag $=32-9-5=18$ bits. The tag only depends on $32-\log_2 16\text{K}$, so it is the same whatever the block size.
examples.answer: Tag 18, index 9, offset 5. Convert block size to bytes before taking the log when addresses are byte addresses.

cards.why: Every cache question starts here. Hit or miss, tag directory size and conflict misses all need the three field widths first. In GATE: it is the most repeated memory pattern, usually as 'find the tag bits' with the block size hidden.
how: Offset $=\log_2(\text{block size in bytes})$.
Lines $=\text{cache size}/\text{block size}$. Index $=\log_2(\text{lines})$.
Tag $=$ address bits $-$ index $-$ offset.
Check: index plus offset must equal $\log_2(\text{cache size})$.
cards.mistake: Subtracting the block bits twice. The cache size already contains the block size, so $\text{tag}=\text{address bits}-\log_2(\text{cache size})$. Another slip is mixing words and bytes for the block size.
edge_cases: Cache size equals block size: one line, index 0 bits.
Word-addressable memory: address bits count words, so the offset counts words, not bytes.
Doubling the block size at a fixed cache size: offset $+1$, index $-1$, tag unchanged.
connections: Set-associative caches (next card) move bits from the index into the tag.
Virtual memory splits an address the same way into page number and page offset (OS: virtual memory).

The cache size doubles and the block size stays fixed. What happens to the tag width?
check.a: It drops by 1 and the index grows by 1.

check.q: A hit needs the line to be valid and which comparison to succeed?
check.a: The stored tag equals the address tag.

cards.title: Set-associative and fully associative caches
cards.simple: Imagine the lockers from before, but now lockers come in groups of four, like a small cupboard with four doors. A student is given a cupboard by the middle digits of their ID, but they can use any of the four doors. This makes fights over one locker rarer. There are fewer cupboards than before, so fewer digits are needed to name the cupboard, and the spare digits go onto the name label. In exam words: a K-way cache has lines divided by K sets. Each doubling of K moves one bit from index to tag. Fully associative means one big cupboard, so no index at all.
cards.idea: A **set-associative** cache groups lines into sets. A block maps to one set, but it may sit in any of the $K$ lines of that set. Fewer sets means fewer index bits. The bits that leave the index join the **tag**. With one set only (fully associative) there is no index at all.
cards.definition:
$\text{sets}=\dfrac{\text{lines}}{K}$, $\text{index}=\log_2(\text{sets})$, $\text{offset}=\log_2(\text{block size})$, $\text{tag}=\text{address bits}-\text{index}-\text{offset}$.

Here $K$ is the number of ways, that is, lines per set. Each doubling of $K$ halves the sets, so the index loses 1 bit and the tag gains 1 bit. Fully associative: $K=\text{lines}$, index $=0$.
cards.intuition_full: Direct mapping gives every block one fixed line, so two busy blocks can keep evicting each other while other lines sit empty. Associativity relaxes this: the index picks a set, and the block may go in any line of the set. The hardware must now compare the tag against $K$ lines in parallel, which costs time and area. The bit bookkeeping is simple. The total lines stay the same, so more ways means fewer sets and fewer index bits. Address length and block size do not change, so the lost index bit has to appear somewhere. It becomes tag, because the tag must now tell apart more blocks that share a set. At the extreme, a fully associative cache has a single set, so the tag is everything above the offset.

examples.setup: A 2 KB cache with 16-byte blocks and 16-bit addresses. Find the tag, index and offset widths for 1, 2, 4, 8 and 128 ways.
steps: Lines $=2048/16=128$. Offset $=4$ bits. Direct mapped (1-way): sets $=128$, index $=7$ bits, tag $=16-7-4=5$ bits.
4-way: sets $=32$, index $=5$, tag $=7$.
8-way: sets $=16$, index $=4$, tag $=8$.
128-way (fully associative): sets $=1$, index $=0$, tag $=16-0-4=12$.
examples.answer: (tag, index): 1-way (5, 7), 2-way (6, 6), 4-way (7, 5), 8-way (8, 4), fully associative (12, 0). Offset stays 4 throughout.

examples.setup: An 8-way set-associative cache has 32-byte blocks. Addresses are 32 bits and the tag is 20 bits. Find the cache size.
steps: Offset $=\log_2 32=5$ bits.
Index $=32-20-5=7$ bits, so there are $2^7=128$ sets.
Lines $=128\times8=1024$.
Cache size $=1024\times32\text{ B}=32\text{ KB}$.
examples.answer: 32 KB. Remember to multiply the sets by the ways to get lines.

examples.setup: A cache has 96 lines and is 3-way set associative with 32-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses. Find the field widths.
steps: Sets $=96/3=32$, which is a power of 2, so the index is $\log_2 32=5$ bits.
Offset $=5$ bits. Tag $=32-5-5=22$ bits.
The ways need not be a power of 2. Only the number of sets must be, for the index to work.
examples.answer: Tag 22, index 5, offset 5. A 3-way cache is fine; a 96-set cache would not be, since 96 is not a power of 2.

cards.why: Associativity cuts conflict misses at the price of wider tags and more comparators. In GATE: find the tag or index width of a K-way cache, or recover the cache size from a given tag width.
how: Lines $=\text{cache size}/\text{block size}$.
Sets $=\text{lines}/K$. Index $=\log_2(\text{sets})$.
Offset $=\log_2(\text{block size})$. Tag is the remaining bits.
Shortcut: from direct mapped to K-way, tag grows by $\log_2 K$.
cards.mistake: Using the direct-mapped index width for a set-associative cache. A 4-way cache with 256 lines has 64 sets, so the index is 6 bits, not 8.
edge_cases: 1-way is direct mapped and $K=\text{lines}$ is fully associative. Same formulas cover both.
Fully associative: index 0 bits, all lookups compare every line.
Total tag storage grows with $K$ because each tag gets longer.
connections: Tag directory size (next card) multiplies this tag width by the number of lines.
Replacement policies (LRU, FIFO) only matter once $K>1$.

cards.what: A **set-associative** cache groups lines into sets. A block maps to one set, but it may sit in any of the $K$ lines of that set. Fewer sets means fewer index bits. The bits that leave the index join the **tag**. With one set only (fully associative) there is no index at all.
cards.what_full:
A **set-associative** cache groups lines into sets. A block maps to one set, but it may sit in any of the $K$ lines of that set. Fewer sets means fewer index bits. The bits that leave the index join the **tag**. With one set only (fully associative) there is no index at all.

$\text{sets}=\dfrac{\text{lines}}{K}$, $\text{index}=\log_2(\text{sets})$, $\text{offset}=\log_2(\text{block size})$, $\text{tag}=\text{address bits}-\text{index}-\text{offset}$.

Here $K$ is the number of ways, that is, lines per set. Each doubling of $K$ halves the sets, so the index loses 1 bit and the tag gains 1 bit. Fully associative: $K=\text{lines}$, index $=0$.

**Worked example.** A 2 KB cache with 16-byte blocks and 16-bit addresses. Find the tag, index and offset widths for 1, 2, 4, 8 and 128 ways.

1. Lines $=2048/16=128$. Offset $=4$ bits. Direct mapped (1-way): sets $=128$, index $=7$ bits, tag $=16-7-4=5$ bits.
2. 2-way: sets $=128/2=64$, index $=6$, tag $=6$.
3. 4-way: sets $=32$, index $=5$, tag $=7$.
4. 8-way: sets $=16$, index $=4$, tag $=8$.
5. 128-way (fully associative): sets $=1$, index $=0$, tag $=16-0-4=12$.

**Answer:** (tag, index): 1-way (5, 7), 2-way (6, 6), 4-way (7, 5), 8-way (8, 4), fully associative (12, 0). Offset stays 4 throughout.

cards.title: Tag directory size
cards.simple: A cache is like a shop shelf with a small sticker on every box. The sticker says which item is inside, and whether the box is valid or has been changed. The boxes themselves are the data. The stickers together are a separate list, and it takes space too. To find how much room the stickers use, count how much one sticker holds and multiply by the number of boxes. In exam words: tag directory size = number of lines times bits per entry. Each entry has the tag plus status bits such as valid and dirty.
cards.idea: The **tag directory** is the table that stores one entry per cache line. Each entry holds the tag plus a few status bits, such as valid and dirty. The size is the number of **lines** times the bits in one entry. The data bytes themselves are not counted.
cards.definition:
$\text{directory size}=\text{lines}\times(\text{tag}+\text{valid}+\text{dirty}+\text{other status bits})$.

Lines $=\text{cache size}/\text{block size}$. The tag width comes from the address split in the previous cards. GATE states which status bits exist, so count exactly those.
cards.intuition_full: The cache stores the data array and the tag directory side by side. The data array is cache size in bytes. The directory is the bookkeeping: for each line it must remember which block is stored (the tag), whether anything is stored (valid), and whether the line differs from memory (dirty, write-back only). A replacement scheme such as LRU may add its own bits. The directory has one entry per line, never per set, because every line carries its own tag and flags. That is why the common slip is to multiply by the set count. A longer tag, from higher associativity or longer addresses, makes every entry wider, so the directory grows.

examples.setup: A 32-bit machine has a 16 KB, 2-way set-associative write-back cache with 64-byte blocks. Each line holds a valid bit and a dirty bit. Find the tag directory size.
steps: Offset $=6$ bits, index $=\log_2 128=7$ bits. Tag $=32-7-6=19$ bits per line.
Add a valid bit to every line: 1 more bit.
Add a dirty bit to every line (write-back cache): 1 more bit.
One entry $=19+1+1=21$ bits.
Directory $=256\times21=5376$ bits. Count lines, not sets.
examples.answer: 5376 bits ($5.25$ Kbit). The data array is separate and holds 16 KB.

examples.setup: A 128 KB, 2-way set-associative, write-back cache has 64-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses. Each directory entry holds the tag, 2 valid bits, 1 modified bit and 1 replacement bit. Find the tag width and the directory size.
steps: Lines $=128\text{K}/64=2048$. Sets $=1024$, so index $=10$ bits. Offset $=6$ bits.
Directory $=2048\times20=40960$ bits $=40$ Kbit.
examples.answer: Tag 16 bits and directory 40 Kbit. Using 1024 sets would give 20 Kbit, which is wrong.

examples.setup: An 8 KB fully associative cache has 32-byte blocks, 24-bit addresses and one valid bit per line. Find the directory size.
steps: Lines $=8192/32=256$. Fully associative: no index, offset $=5$ bits.
Tag $=24-5=19$ bits. Entry $=19+1=20$ bits.
Directory $=256\times20=5120$ bits.
examples.answer: 5120 bits. With no index the whole block number is the tag, so a fully associative directory is the widest per entry.

cards.why: It tells you how much extra storage a cache design costs beyond its data array. In GATE: compute directory size from cache size, ways, block size, address width and the stated status bits.
how: Find lines $=\text{cache size}/\text{block size}$.
Get the tag width from the address split.
Entry width $=\text{tag}+$ every status bit named in the stem.
Directory $=\text{lines}\times\text{entry width}$.
cards.mistake: Counting sets instead of lines. Each line has its own tag, so multiply by lines. Do not add the dirty bit if the cache is write-through, and do not add bits the stem does not mention.
edge_cases: Write-through caches have no dirty bit.
Replacement bits can be per line or per set. Read the stem and follow it.
Direct mapped needs no replacement bits.
connections: Uses the tag width from cards m2 and m3.
Write-back and dirty bits are explained in the write policies card (m8).

check.q: 16-bit address, 1 KB direct mapped, 32 B blocks, valid bit only. Directory size?
Does the 16 KB of data count in the directory size?
check.a: No. The directory holds tags and flags only.

check.q: Two caches have the same size and block size. One is direct mapped, one is 4-way. Which directory is larger?
check.a: The 4-way one, because its tags are 2 bits longer.

cards.title: Average memory access time, one level
cards.simple: You need a pencil 25 times today. Usually it is in your bag and takes 2 seconds. Twice it is missing and you run to the shop, which costs 40 extra seconds. Add all the waiting and divide by 25 to get your average wait, 5.2 seconds. In exam words: the average memory access time (AMAT) is the hit time plus the miss rate times the miss penalty.
cards.idea: The **average memory access time (AMAT)** is the average cost of one memory access. Every access pays the hit time. The few that miss also pay a penalty. So the average is the hit time plus the miss rate times the penalty.
cards.definition:
$\text{AMAT}=t_{hit}+m\times P$

Here $t_{hit}$ is the time to look in the cache, $m$ is the miss rate (misses divided by accesses) and $P$ is the extra time a miss adds. If the stem gives the full time of a miss, $t_{miss}$, lookup included, use $\text{AMAT}=h\,t_{hit}+(1-h)\,t_{miss}$ with hit ratio $h=1-m$.
cards.intuition_full: AMAT is a weighted average. Hits happen a fraction $h$ of the time and cost $t_{hit}$. Misses happen the rest of the time and cost the full miss time. If a miss time is the lookup plus a penalty, then $h\,t+(1-h)(t+P)=t+(1-h)P$, which is the short formula. So the short formula is right only when $P$ is the extra on top of the lookup. The real difficulty is wording. 'Miss penalty' means extra time. 'Time to service a miss' or 'access time on a miss' is often the whole thing. Draw one miss on a timeline and ask whether the cache lookup already sits inside the number you were given. The answer must always lie between the hit time and the miss time.

examples.setup: A cache has hit time 2 cycles, miss penalty 40 cycles and miss rate 8%. Find the AMAT by following 25 accesses.
steps: Take 25 accesses. The miss rate is 8%, so 2 miss and 23 hit.
Every access pays the hit time of 2 cycles, hit or miss: $25\times2=50$ cycles.
Each of the 2 misses also pays the 40-cycle penalty: $2\times40=80$ cycles.
Total time $=50+80=130$ cycles.
Average per access $=130/25=5.2$ cycles.
The formula gives the same value: $\text{AMAT}=2+0.08\times40=5.2$.
examples.answer: $\text{AMAT}=5.2$ cycles.

examples.setup: The hit ratio is 0.95 and the hit time is 4 ns. A miss takes 100 ns in total, and this figure already includes the cache lookup. Find the AMAT.
steps: The 100 ns is a total miss time, not an extra penalty. Use the weighted form.
Cross-check with the penalty form: the extra is $100-4=96$ ns, so $4+0.05\times96=8.8$ ns.
examples.answer: 8.8 ns. Adding 4 ns on top of a total of 100 ns would give 9 ns, which is wrong.

examples.setup: A cache of 5 ns is checked first, and only on a miss is memory (60 ns) started. The hit ratio is 0.9. Find the AMAT.
steps: A miss does the cache lookup first, then the memory read: $5+60=65$ ns in total.
$\text{AMAT}=0.9\times5+0.1\times65=4.5+6.5=11$ ns.
Using 60 ns as the miss time would give $4.5+6=10.5$ ns. That drops the lookup the miss also paid.
examples.answer: 11 ns. When the lookup comes first, a miss pays for both the lookup and the memory read.

cards.why: AMAT turns hit rates into a single performance number, and every later cache question builds on it. In GATE: a hit ratio and two access times, usually 1 to 2 marks, where the wording decides whether the lookup is counted twice.
how: List hit time, miss rate (or hit ratio) and the miss figure.
Decide if the miss figure is an extra penalty or a full miss time.
Penalty: $t_{hit}+m\,P$. Full time: $h\,t_{hit}+(1-h)\,t_{miss}$.
Sanity check: the answer lies between the hit time and the miss time.
cards.mistake: Adding the hit time to a miss time that is already a total, or leaving it out when the figure is only a penalty. Ask whether the lookup is already inside the number.
edge_cases: Miss rate 0: AMAT equals the hit time.
Miss rate 1: AMAT equals the full miss time (hit time plus penalty).
Hit ratio given as a percentage: turn it into a fraction first.
Cache and memory started together (parallel lookup): the miss time is just the memory time.
connections: Two levels nest this formula (next card).
CPI with stalls (card m7) uses the same product of miss rate and penalty.

check.q: Hit time 1 ns, miss rate 10%, penalty 20 ns. AMAT?
Hit ratio 0.8, hit time 2 ns, a miss takes 50 ns in total. AMAT?
Can the AMAT ever be below the hit time?
check.a: No. Every access pays at least the hit time.

cards.title: Multi-level AMAT and local miss rates
cards.simple: Every time you look something up, you check your desk first. Only if the desk fails do you walk to the shelf, and only if the shelf fails do you go to the city library. So the shelf trip is paid only by the lookups that failed at the desk, and the city trip only by those that failed at both. To get the average wait, weight each trip by how many lookups reach it. In exam words: AMAT = t1 + m1 (t2 + m2 · t_mem), where m2 is the local miss rate, the share of L2 accesses that miss.
cards.idea: Cache levels are tried in order. Every access pays L1's time. Only L1 misses go on to pay L2's time. Only L2 misses go on to pay memory's time. So AMAT nests: each deeper level is weighted by the chance of reaching it.
cards.definition:
$\text{AMAT}=t_1+m_1\,(t_2+m_2\,t_{mem})$

Here $m_1$ is the L1 miss rate. $m_2$ is the **local** L2 miss rate: L2 misses divided by L2 accesses, which equal L1 misses. The **global** L2 miss rate is $m_1\times m_2$: L2 misses divided by all accesses.
cards.intuition_full: Follow 1000 accesses down the levels. All 1000 touch L1. Only the $1000\,m_1$ that miss touch L2. Only the $1000\,m_1m_2$ that miss again touch memory. The time spent is the sum of count times level time, and dividing by 1000 gives the formula. A local rate is conditional: it is the miss rate among accesses that actually reached that level. A global rate is unconditional: misses per original access. Global is the product of the local rates down the chain. The stem may give either kind, so convert first. A good habit is to write the counts per 1000 accesses, as the scene does, because it makes the weights visible and stops you from mixing the two rates.

examples.setup: L1 has hit time 1 ns and miss rate 8%. L2 has hit time 6 ns and local miss rate 25%. Memory takes 80 ns. Find the AMAT and the global L2 miss rate.
steps: Send 1000 accesses to L1. Every one pays L1's 1 ns: $1000\times1=1000$ ns.
L1 misses 8% of them, so 80 accesses go on to L2.
Those 80 pay L2's 6 ns: $80\times6=480$ ns.
L2's local miss rate is 25% of the 80 it sees, so 20 accesses reach memory.
Those 20 pay memory's 80 ns: $20\times80=1600$ ns.
examples.answer: $\text{AMAT}=3.08$ ns. The global L2 miss rate is $0.08\times0.25=2\%$ (20 of 1000).

examples.setup: L1 hit time is 2 cycles, L2 hit time 10 cycles, memory 100 cycles. L1 misses on 5% of all accesses, and L2 misses on 1% of all accesses (a global rate). Find the AMAT.
steps: The 1% is global. The local L2 miss rate is $1\%/5\%=0.2$.
Cross-check with global rates: $2+0.05\times10+0.01\times100=2+0.5+1=3.5$ cycles.
examples.answer: 3.5 cycles. Using 1% as the local rate would give $2+0.05(10+1)=2.55$, which is wrong.

examples.setup: Three levels: $t_1=1$, $m_1=0.10$, $t_2=4$, $m_2=0.50$, $t_3=20$, $m_3=0.40$, memory 200 cycles. Find the AMAT.
steps: Work from the inside out. Memory term: $t_3+m_3\,t_{mem}=20+0.4\times200=100$.
Outer: $t_1+m_1\times54=1+0.1\times54=6.4$.
examples.answer: 6.4 cycles. The nesting extends: $t_1+m_1(t_2+m_2(t_3+m_3\,t_{mem}))$.

cards.why: Real machines have two or three cache levels, and GATE tests whether you can nest them without mixing local and global rates. In GATE: find AMAT, or find a miss rate given an AMAT or a count of misses per instruction.
how: Write the chain: $t_1$, $m_1$, $t_2$, $m_2$, $t_{mem}$.
Turn any global rate into a local one: local $=$ this level's global rate $\div$ the previous level's global rate.
Compute inside out: first $t_2+m_2\,t_{mem}$, then multiply by $m_1$ and add $t_1$.

L1 miss rate 0: L2 and memory never matter.

cards.title: CPI with memory stalls
cards.simple: Say a student normally finishes one homework question in 1.2 minutes when everything is on the desk. Every question needs a worksheet, and one question in four also needs a textbook. Now and then the worksheet or textbook is not on the desk and the student walks to the shelf, which costs 30 minutes. The extra time per question is how often the lookups happen, times how often they fail, times the walk. In exam words: effective CPI = base CPI + memory stall cycles per instruction, where stalls = references per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty.
cards.idea: Cycles per instruction (**CPI**) with a perfect cache is the base CPI. Each cache miss stalls the processor for the miss penalty. Add the stall cycles per instruction to the base. Stalls per instruction are references per instruction times miss rate times penalty.
cards.definition:
$\text{CPI}=\text{CPI}_{base}+\text{(refs per instruction)}\times m\times P$.

With separate caches: $\text{CPI}=\text{CPI}_{base}+m_I\,P+f_{mem}\,m_D\,P$. Every instruction is fetched, so the instruction term has 1 reference per instruction. Only loads and stores, a fraction $f_{mem}$ of instructions, use the data cache. $P$ is the miss penalty in cycles.
cards.intuition_full: The processor runs at the base CPI until it misses, then it waits. Waiting is lost cycles, spread over all instructions. So the extra CPI is just the average number of stall cycles per instruction. Count the references that can miss, per instruction. Instruction fetch happens for every instruction, so it always contributes. Data accesses happen only for loads and stores. Multiply each count by its miss rate and the penalty, then add. A speedup between two machines that differ only in memory is the ratio of their CPIs, because instruction count and clock cycle are the same. If the stem gives misses per 1000 instructions, that number already includes the references, so do not multiply by references again.

examples.setup: Base CPI is 1.2. The instruction cache misses 2% of fetches and the data cache misses 6% of data accesses. 25% of instructions are loads or stores. The miss penalty is 30 cycles. Find the CPI and the speedup of a perfect cache.
steps: With a perfect cache every instruction takes the base CPI, 1.2 cycles.
Every instruction is fetched. Fetch stalls $=1\times0.02\times30=0.6$ cycles per instruction.
Only 25% of instructions are loads or stores. Data stalls $=0.25\times0.06\times30=0.45$.
A perfect cache would give 1.2, so the speedup is $2.25/1.2=1.875$.
examples.answer: Effective CPI $=2.25$. A perfect cache would be $1.875\times$ faster.

examples.setup: Base CPI is 1.0. 26% of instructions are loads and 10% are stores. The instruction cache miss rate is 1% and the data cache miss rate is 4%. The penalty is 100 cycles. Find the CPI.
steps: Fetch stalls $=1\times0.01\times100=1.0$.
Memory instructions $=26\%+10\%=36\%$, so data stalls $=0.36\times0.04\times100=1.44$.
examples.answer: $\text{CPI}=3.44$. Applying the 4% data miss rate to every instruction would give 6.0, which is wrong.

examples.setup: Base CPI is 1.0. The instruction cache has 5 misses per 1000 instructions and the data cache has 15 misses per 1000 instructions. The penalty is 100 cycles. Find the CPI.
steps: The figures are already per instruction, so no reference count is needed.
Stalls $=\dfrac{5+15}{1000}\times100=2.0$ cycles per instruction.

cards.title: Write policies
cards.simple: You edit a notice on your phone, which is a copy of the master on the school wall. One way is to walk to the wall and fix the master after every single edit. That is slow but the wall is always correct. The other way is to edit only your copy and put a red mark on it. You walk to the wall only when you must throw the copy away. If you edit the same notice ten times, you make one trip instead of ten. In exam words: write-through updates memory on every write. Write-back sets a dirty bit and writes memory only when a dirty line is evicted.
cards.idea: A **write policy** decides when changed data reaches main memory. **Write-through** updates memory on every write. **Write-back** updates only the cache and sets a **dirty** bit, then writes the block to memory when it is evicted. A second choice, allocation, decides whether a write miss loads the block.
cards.definition:
Write-through: every write goes to the cache and to memory; no dirty bit is needed. Write-back: a write hit changes only the cache and sets the dirty bit; a dirty line is written to memory on eviction.

Write-allocate: on a write miss, load the block, then write it. No-write-allocate: on a write miss, write memory only and leave the cache alone. Write-back caches usually allocate on a write miss.
cards.intuition_full: Memory traffic is the cost to watch. Write-through is simple and keeps memory always current, but every store pays a memory trip, so a write buffer is often added. Write-back saves trips when a block is written many times before it is evicted, because only the last version travels. The price is the dirty bit and a slower eviction of dirty lines. The dirty bit exists only in write-back caches. Allocation is independent: it only affects what a write miss does. Write-allocate bets that the block will be used again soon. No-write-allocate bets that written data is not read soon, as in a log being written out. To count memory writes, trace the accesses and track, per line, which block is held and whether it is dirty.

cards.title: Replacement policies and miss types
cards.simple: Your school bag fits only 3 books. When you need a fourth, one has to come out. Rule one (LRU): take out the book you have not touched for the longest time. Rule two (FIFO): take out the book that has been in the bag the longest, even if you used it a minute ago. A miss also has a reason. It is the first time you need that book, or the bag is simply too small, or the book got pushed out only because of a fixed-slot rule. In exam words: LRU evicts the least recently used block and FIFO the oldest loaded block. The misses are compulsory, capacity or conflict.
cards.idea: When a set is full, a **replacement policy** picks the victim. **LRU** evicts the block unused for the longest time. **FIFO** evicts the block loaded longest ago, even if it was used since. Misses come in three kinds: **compulsory** (first touch), **capacity** (cache too small) and **conflict** (too many blocks want one set).
cards.definition:
LRU: on every access move the block to the newest end; evict from the oldest end. FIFO: order by load time only; a hit does not change the order.

A miss is compulsory if the block was never accessed before. Otherwise it is a capacity miss if a fully associative cache of the same size would also miss, and a conflict miss if that cache would have hit.
cards.intuition_full: LRU bets on temporal locality: a block used recently will be used again soon, so the block unused for longest is the safest to drop. FIFO ignores hits, so it can throw out a block that is used constantly. FIFO can even miss more after you add lines (Belady's anomaly), whereas LRU cannot, because the contents of a smaller LRU cache are always inside a larger one. To simulate, keep each set's lines and an order list. A hit moves the block to the newest end in LRU and changes nothing in FIFO. In a set-associative cache the policy runs separately inside each set. The miss kinds tell you which fix helps. Compulsory misses need prefetching or bigger blocks, capacity misses need a bigger cache and conflict misses need more associativity.

examples.setup: A fully associative cache has 3 lines, starts empty and uses LRU. The block accesses are 2, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2, 4, 3. Find the hits and the misses, and name each miss.
steps: Access 2: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). A line is free, so load it. Order: 2.
Access 3: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). A line is free, so load it. Order: 2, 3.
Access 2: it is in the cache, a hit. Move it to the newest end of the order: 3, 2.
Access 1: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). A line is free, so load it. Order: 3, 2, 1.
Access 5: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). The oldest in the order is 3, so evict it and load 5. Order: 2, 1, 5.
Access 2: it is in the cache, a hit. Move it to the newest end of the order: 1, 5, 2.
Access 4: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). The oldest in the order is 1, so evict it and load 4. Order: 5, 2, 4.

Access 3: not in the cache, a capacity miss (it was evicted earlier and a fully associative cache of 3 lines also misses). The oldest in the order is 5, so evict it and load 3. Order: 2, 4, 3. Totals: 6 misses and 2 hits.
examples.answer: 6 misses (5 compulsory, 1 capacity) and 2 hits. FIFO on the same trace misses 7 times.

examples.setup: A cache has 4 lines, is 2-way set associative (2 sets) and uses LRU. Block $b$ goes to set $b \bmod 2$. The accesses are 0, 2, 4, 0, 2, 4, 1, 3, 1. How many conflict misses are there?

Set 0 holds 2 blocks. The first round 0, 2, 4 misses 3 times (compulsory). Loading 4 evicts 0, so the next 0 misses and evicts 2, the next 2 misses and evicts 4, and the next 4 misses and evicts 0: 3 more misses.
Set 1: 1 misses, 3 misses (both compulsory), then 1 hits.
Total misses $=6+2=8$. Distinct blocks $=5$, so 5 are compulsory.
A fully associative 4-line LRU cache holds 0, 2, 4 together, so it hits on the second 0, 2, 4. Those 3 misses are conflict misses.
examples.answer: 3 conflict misses (5 compulsory, 0 capacity). The 3 non-compulsory misses all come from set 0 being too small for 3 blocks.

examples.setup: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines. Block $b$ goes to line $b \bmod 4$. The accesses are 0, 4, 0, 4, 0, 4. Count and classify the misses.
steps: Blocks 0 and 4 both map to line 0. Lines 1, 2 and 3 stay empty the whole time.
Every access misses: 6 misses. Only 2 are first touches.
A fully associative cache would hold both blocks and hit, so the other 4 are conflict misses, not capacity misses.

cards.title: Block transfer and interleaving
cards.simple: You ask a friend in another city to post you 4 photos. The first one takes 30 minutes because they must find the album. After that they hand over a photo every 6 minutes. The whole set takes 30 + 3 × 6 = 48 minutes. Now imagine four friends each send one photo at the same time. All four come together after one wait. That is why memory is split into banks. In exam words: the penalty for a block of w words is the first-word time plus (w − 1) times the next-word time. With interleaved banks, consecutive words sit in different banks, so one round delivers several words.
cards.idea: A cache miss moves a whole **block**, several words, not one. The first word is slow. Later words come faster if memory can burst them. **Interleaving** splits memory into banks so that consecutive words sit in different banks and are read at the same time.
cards.definition:
Burst memory: $P=t_{first}+(w-1)\,t_{next}$ for a block of $w$ words.

With $n$ interleaved banks that each take $t_b$ per access, one round gives $n$ consecutive words. A $w$-word block needs $\lceil w/n\rceil$ rounds, so $P=\lceil w/n\rceil\,t_b$, plus any address or bus time the stem adds. One non-interleaved module needs $w\,t_b$. Word $k$ lives in bank $k \bmod n$.
cards.intuition_full: A DRAM read has a long set-up for the first word. Words in the same row then stream out quickly. That is the burst picture, $t_{first}+(w-1)t_{next}$. Interleaving gets a similar speed-up by using several small memory modules side by side. Word $k$ sits in bank $k \bmod n$, so a block of consecutive words touches every bank once and all banks work at the same time. The block then costs about one bank time per $n$ words instead of one per word, a speed-up of up to $n$. It breaks when the access pattern keeps hitting the same bank. A stride that is a multiple of $n$ sends every access to bank 0, and the banks wait in a queue. Read the stem carefully for extras such as an address-send time or a bus transfer time per word.

examples.setup: A block has 4 words. Memory delivers the first word after 30 ns and each later word 6 ns after the previous one. Hit time is 2 ns and miss rate is 4%. Find the miss penalty and the AMAT.
steps: The miss starts at time 0. Memory needs 30 ns to find and deliver the first word.
Word 1 arrives at 30 ns. Later words in the same burst follow 6 ns apart.
Word 2 arrives at $30+6=36$ ns.
Word 3 arrives at $36+6=42$ ns.
Word 4 arrives at $42+6=48$ ns. The block is complete: penalty $=30+3\times6=48$ ns.
With hit time 2 ns and miss rate 4%: $\text{AMAT}=2+0.04\times48=3.92$ ns.
examples.answer: Miss penalty 48 ns and $\text{AMAT}=3.92$ ns.

examples.setup: Main memory has 4 interleaved banks, each taking 60 ns per access. A cache block has 16 consecutive words. Hit time is 5 ns and miss rate 2%. Find the AMAT, and compare with a single non-interleaved module.
steps: One round gives 4 words. Rounds $=16/4=4$, so the penalty is $4\times60=240$ ns.
$\text{AMAT}=5+0.02\times240=9.8$ ns.
Non-interleaved: $16\times60=960$ ns per block, so $\text{AMAT}=5+0.02\times960=24.2$ ns.
examples.answer: 9.8 ns interleaved against 24.2 ns without interleaving, a block speed-up of 4.

examples.setup: The same 4 banks (60 ns each, word $k$ in bank $k \bmod 4$). The CPU reads words 0, 4, 8, 12 in order. How long does that take, compared with reading words 0, 1, 2, 3?
steps: Words 0, 4, 8, 12 all have $k \bmod 4=0$, so all four live in bank 0.
One bank serves one access at a time: $4\times60=240$ ns.
Words 0, 1, 2, 3 sit in four different banks and arrive together after one round: 60 ns.
examples.answer: 240 ns against 60 ns. Interleaving only helps when the access pattern spreads across banks.

cards.title: Locality and array traversal
cards.simple: In a library, if you read a book page after page, one trip to fetch it gives you many pages. If you read page 1 of a different book every time, you make a new trip for every read, and your small desk cannot hold all those books. A program that walks along a row of an array is like reading page after page. Walking down a column is like jumping to a new book each time. In exam words: row-major order has spatial locality, so one miss per block. A column scan jumps a whole row each step and can miss on every access, especially when the row length is a power of two and the jumps all land on the same few cache lines.
cards.idea: **Locality** is why caches work. **Spatial locality**: after touching an address you soon touch its neighbours, so loading a block pays off. **Temporal locality**: you touch the same address again soon. A C array is stored **row-major**, so scanning a row walks neighbours, while scanning a column jumps a whole row each step.
cards.definition:
Row-major: $A[i][j]$ is at $\text{base}+(i\cdot\text{cols}+j)\cdot s$, where $s$ is the element size in bytes.

Row scan, cold cache: one miss per block, so misses $=\dfrac{\text{elements}\times s}{\text{block size}}$ when the whole array streams through. Column scan: consecutive reads are $\text{cols}\cdot s$ bytes apart. If this stride is a multiple of the way size (cache size over ways), all reads fall in the same set and keep evicting each other.
cards.intuition_full: A block is a free gift of neighbours. A row scan uses every gift: for 4-byte ints and 64-byte blocks, 16 reads for one miss. A column scan throws the gifts away. It takes one int from each block and moves on, and by the time it comes back for the next column the block may be gone. Whether it is gone depends on the stride. When the row length in bytes is a multiple of the cache way size, every read in a column maps to the same set, so even a large cache cannot keep them. This is why people pad array rows by one block. Temporal locality works on the other axis: a loop that re-reads a small array many times keeps hitting, as long as the array fits and does not collide with other data.

A[0][4] starts block 1: one miss. A[0][5] to A[0][7] hit. Row 0 cost 2 misses for 8 reads.
Scanning all 8 rows: 64 reads, 16 misses (one per block), 48 hits. Miss rate 25%.
Column scan from an empty cache. A[0][0] is block 0 (line 0): miss. A[1][0] is block 2 (line 2): miss. They are a whole row (32 bytes) apart, so they sit in different blocks.
A[2][0] is block 4, which also maps to line 0, so it evicts block 0. A[3][0] is block 6, line 2, evicts block 2. Only lines 0 and 2 are used in this column.
After column 0: 8 reads, 8 misses. Column 1 starts with A[0][1], block 0, which was evicted. Miss again. Each column reloads the same 8 blocks.
Column scan total: 64 reads, 64 misses. That is 4 times the row scan, because no read ever finds its block still cached.

cards.title: DRAM refresh overhead
cards.simple: Imagine a row of 8192 tiny buckets of water, each with a slow leak. If you do not top up a bucket within 64 milliseconds, it runs dry and the data is lost. Topping up one bucket takes 50 nanoseconds. So you go along the whole row, topping up each in turn, and then start again. The time you spend topping up, as a share of the 64 ms you are allowed, is tiny. In exam words: refresh overhead = rows × time per row refresh ÷ refresh period. Several chips refresh together, so adding chips does not add time.
cards.idea: A **DRAM** cell stores a bit as charge in a leaky capacitor. The charge fades, so every row must be read and rewritten, **refreshed**, within a fixed period. The refresh overhead is the share of time the chip spends doing this: rows times the time per row, divided by the period.
cards.definition:
$\text{overhead}=\dfrac{R\times t_{row}}{T}$

Here $R$ is the number of rows to refresh, $t_{row}$ is the time to refresh one row and $T$ is the refresh period within which every row must be refreshed once. Chips refresh in parallel, so the overhead of a memory of several identical chips equals that of one chip. With distributed refresh one row is refreshed every $T/R$.
cards.intuition_full: The data is only safe if every row is refreshed at least once per period $T$. One pass over all rows costs $R\times t_{row}$. That pass happens once per period, so the busy fraction is the cost of one pass divided by $T$. It is a duty cycle, like a guard walking the same round every hour. Two common schemes spread the work differently. Burst refresh does all rows together, blocking the memory for the full pass. Distributed refresh does one row every $T/R$, so each stall is only $t_{row}$ long. The total share of time is identical. All the chips of a memory receive the refresh together, so the fraction does not multiply with the chip count.

examples.setup: A DRAM chip has 8192 rows. Refreshing one row takes 50 ns. Every row must be refreshed once every 64 ms. Find the fraction of time spent on refresh, and the fraction for a memory of 4 such chips.
steps: A DRAM bit is a tiny leaky capacitor, so every row must be refreshed within 64 ms. This chip has 8192 rows.
Refreshing one row takes 50 ns.
Refreshing all rows once: $8192\times50\text{ ns}=409{,}600\text{ ns}=409.6\ \mu\text{s}$.
The refresh period is 64 ms $=64{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$.
Fraction of time spent refreshing $=409.6/64{,}000=0.64\%$.
A memory made of 4 such chips refreshes them in parallel, so the overhead is still 0.64%, not 4 times as much.
examples.answer: 0.64% for one chip and also 0.64% for four chips.

examples.setup: A DRAM chip has 16384 rows, a row refresh takes 45 ns, and each row must be refreshed once every 32 ms. What percentage of time is spent refreshing?
steps: One pass $=16384\times45\text{ ns}=737{,}280\text{ ns}=737.28\ \mu\text{s}$.
Period $=32\text{ ms}=32{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$.
examples.answer: 2.304%, which rounds to 2.30%. Keep the units consistent: ns against ms is the usual slip.

examples.setup: Same chip (16384 rows, 45 ns per row, 32 ms period) uses distributed refresh. How often is a row refreshed, and how long is each stall?

Each refresh stalls the chip for 45 ns.
Check: $45/1953.125=2.304\%$, the same overhead as the burst scheme.
examples.answer: A row every $1.953\ \mu\text{s}$ with 45 ns stalls. The total share is the same 2.304%, but the longest stall is far shorter.

Access 3: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). A line is free, so load it. Order: 2, 3.
Access 2: it is in the cache, a hit. Move it to the newest end of the order: 3, 2.
Access 1: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). A line is free, so load it. Order: 3, 2, 1.
Access 5: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). The oldest in the order is 3, so evict it and load 5. Order: 2, 1, 5.
Access 2: it is in the cache, a hit. Move it to the newest end of the order: 1, 5, 2.
Access 4: not in the cache, a compulsory miss (first touch). The oldest in the order is 1, so evict it and load 4. Order: 5, 2, 4.

Access 3: not in the cache, a capacity miss (it was evicted earlier and a fully associative cache of 3 lines also misses). The oldest in the order is 5, so evict it and load 3. Order: 2, 4, 3. Totals: 6 misses and 2 hits.

scenes.title: A four-word block arriving on a timeline

objects.text: 4 words: first 30 ns, then 6 ns apart

steps.caption: The miss starts at time 0. Memory needs 30 ns to find and deliver the first word.
Word 1 arrives at 30 ns. Later words in the same burst follow 6 ns apart.
Word 2 arrives at $30+6=36$ ns.
Word 3 arrives at $36+6=42$ ns.
Word 4 arrives at $42+6=48$ ns. The block is complete: penalty $=30+3\times6=48$ ns.
With hit time 2 ns and miss rate 4%: $\text{AMAT}=2+0.04\times48=3.92$ ns.

scenes.title: Row scan versus column scan of a small array

objects.text: int A[8][8], 4 B ints, 16 B blocks, 4 lines

steps.caption: The array is 8 by 8, stored row by row (row-major). A 16-byte block holds 4 neighbouring ints of one row, so the array is 16 blocks; the cells show their block numbers. Block $b$ goes to line $b \bmod 4$.
Row scan, A[0][0]: block 0 is not in line 0, so it misses and loads. A[0][1], A[0][2], A[0][3] are in the same block: 3 hits.
A[0][4] starts block 1: one miss. A[0][5] to A[0][7] hit. Row 0 cost 2 misses for 8 reads.
Scanning all 8 rows: 64 reads, 16 misses (one per block), 48 hits. Miss rate 25%.
Column scan from an empty cache. A[0][0] is block 0 (line 0): miss. A[1][0] is block 2 (line 2): miss. They are a whole row (32 bytes) apart, so they sit in different blocks.
A[2][0] is block 4, which also maps to line 0, so it evicts block 0. A[3][0] is block 6, line 2, evicts block 2. Only lines 0 and 2 are used in this column.
After column 0: 8 reads, 8 misses. Column 1 starts with A[0][1], block 0, which was evicted. Miss again. Each column reloads the same 8 blocks.
Column scan total: 64 reads, 64 misses. That is 4 times the row scan, because no read ever finds its block still cached.

scenes.title: DRAM refresh as a slice of the refresh period

steps.caption: A DRAM bit is a tiny leaky capacitor, so every row must be refreshed within 64 ms. This chip has 8192 rows.

set.text: each row needs a refresh every 64 ms

steps.caption: Refreshing one row takes 50 ns.
Refreshing all rows once: $8192\times50\text{ ns}=409{,}600\text{ ns}=409.6\ \mu\text{s}$.
The refresh period is 64 ms $=64{,}000\ \mu\text{s}$.
Fraction of time spent refreshing $=409.6/64{,}000=0.64\%$.
